opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think context is one of the most natural levers we have, but I'd be careful not to equate a longer context window with long-horizon learning. They're related, but they're not the same thing.

A bigger context window gives the model more working memory. If you're doing a multi-hour task, debugging a large codebase or running a long research workflow, being able to keep a lot of history in view matters. The model can refer back to what it tried, what failed, and what the user said three hours ago. That's real, and we've seen capabilities unlock as context gets longer and, more importantly, as the model actually *uses* that context well. Advertising a million tokens is easy. Getting a model that reasons coherently across all of them is the hard part.

But when people say "long-horizon learning," I think they often mean something more like what a person does on the job. You start somewhere new, and over weeks you build intuition, you learn the codebase, you learn your teammates' preferences, and you get better. Some of that is memory, but a lot of it is something closer to consolidation. You're not rereading every past experience every time. You've distilled it.

So I see a spectrum. On one end is pure in-context learning, where you stuff everything in and let attention handle it. On the other end is updating the weights. In between are things like retrieval, learned memory, summarization, and the model writing notes for itself. I suspect the answer is some mix of these. Context length is necessary, because you need enough room to do coherent work within a single episode. But I don't think it's sufficient on its own, partly for cost reasons and partly because raw history isn't the same as learned understanding.

The other piece I'd emphasize is that the training has to reward using long context well. If you train mostly on short tasks, it doesn't matter how long the window is. The model won't have learned to plan over that horizon or to recover from mistakes it made earlier. So for me the interesting work is less "make the window bigger" and more "build tasks and training signals where long horizons actually matter," and then see what kind of memory the model needs to succeed at them.

r001.rationale: The response separates having a larger window from using it effectively: it says more context provides working memory, but coherent reasoning across that context is the hard part.

r002.rationale: It describes distilling past experience instead of rereading it all, and names summarization and self-written notes as memory approaches between raw context and weight updates.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think context window is one of those things that people sometimes conflate with learning, and I'd want to separate them a little bit.

A longer context window is really about how much the model can attend to at inference time. It's working memory. And that's genuinely useful for long-horizon tasks, right? If you're doing an agentic coding task that spans hours, you want the model to remember what it tried twenty steps ago, what the error messages were, what constraints the user gave you at the beginning. So in that narrow sense, yes, more context lets you operate over longer horizons without losing the thread.

But I don't think it's the same thing as learning. Learning, to me, means the model is actually updating something, getting better at a task in a way that persists and generalizes. Context is more like a scratchpad. You can put a lot of stuff on the scratchpad, and the model can do in-context learning off of it, which is real and surprisingly powerful. But when the episode ends, nothing has changed about the model itself.

And there's a practical issue too, which is that just because you can fit a million tokens in doesn't mean the model is using them well. We've seen this a lot. Retrieval quality degrades, the model gets distracted by irrelevant stuff, and you end up with these needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks that look great but don't reflect how the model actually reasons over the whole context when the task is hard.

So my view is that context window is necessary but not sufficient. What I'm more excited about for long-horizon learning is the combination: long context plus reasoning, where the model can spend compute deciding what in that context actually matters, plus some mechanism for distilling experience back into the model, whether that's through training on its own trajectories or some form of memory that's more structured than just raw tokens. I think the interesting frontier is less "how many tokens can we fit" and more "how does the model decide what to keep and how does that compound over time."

r001.rationale: It distinguishes a longer window’s capacity to hold context from using that context effectively, noting retrieval degradation and distraction by irrelevant material.

r002.rationale: It mentions structured memory and distilling experience into the model, but does not identify compaction of the model’s working state as a way to support long-horizon learning.

astra-6.text:
I think a longer context window is one way to make progress on that, because it lets the model carry more of its experience forward. It can see what it tried, what feedback it got, and potentially adapt its approach without changing its weights.

But I’d distinguish having a longer context from actually learning effectively from it. If you give a model a huge history, can it identify the important parts? Can it recognize that an approach failed and avoid repeating it? Can it take something it learned early on and apply it much later? Those are capabilities you need to develop, beyond just making the window bigger.

So I see context as an enabling piece. The deeper question is how you turn that accumulated experience into better decisions over a long horizon.

r001.rationale: It explicitly distinguishes a larger context window from the separate capabilities needed to use accumulated history effectively.

r002.rationale: It mentions carrying experience in context, but does not identify compaction of working state as a way to support long-horizon learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a longer context window is one way to let a model learn from experience without changing its weights. You can give it a task, let it try things, and keep the outcomes in context so it can adjust what it does next. As you extend that window, you potentially extend the horizon over which that adaptation can happen.

But fitting more tokens isn’t sufficient. The model has to use that history effectively: recognize which attempts failed, extract something useful from them, and apply it much later. Otherwise, you just have a longer transcript.

So I’d separate the capacity to retain experience from the ability to learn from it. Longer context gives you room for the former. You still need training and evaluations that push on the latter.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes having room to retain experience in a longer context from effectively learning from and applying that history.

r002.rationale: It does not identify compaction of working state as a way to support long-horizon learning.
